analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on offshore tax havens and loopholes that let corporations and wealthy individuals shift profits overseas.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2017 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given the Treasury Department new tools to penalize foreign banks and countries that block U.S. tax enforcement. It would have tightened rules that let U.S. companies move profits and patents to low-tax countries, required large corporations to report their profits, employees, and taxes country by country, and extended anti-money-laundering rules to investment advisers and company formation agents. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit if the bill passes, because income that corporations and wealthy individuals shelter offshore would face U.S. tax, broadening the base that funds public services and reducing pressure on other taxpayers to make up the difference. Honest domestic businesses that pay full U.S. taxes would also compete on a more level field against rivals that shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions.

how_it_helps.text: It would let Treasury restrict correspondent banking and card services for foreign jurisdictions and institutions that significantly impede U.S. tax enforcement, not just money laundering [S2].
It would treat foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic for tax purposes, closing the route of moving a headquarters on paper to a low-tax country [S2].

It would tax excess profits from patents and other intangibles shifted to low-taxed foreign affiliates, and tighten rules on corporate 'inversions' — U.S. companies acquiring foreign firms to reincorporate abroad [S2].
It would require public companies to disclose revenues, profits, taxes paid, and employees on a country-by-country basis, making it visible when profits are booked in tax havens [S2].
It would impose anti-money-laundering obligations on investment advisers and on businesses that form companies, trusts, and LLCs, which are common channels for hiding ownership [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations using offshore profit-shifting and tax inversions, wealthy individuals hiding assets in non-cooperating foreign institutions, offshore financial and trust service providers, and hedge funds and investment advisers newly subject to anti-money-laundering rules would bear the cost in taxes, penalties, and compliance.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose significant new compliance and reporting costs on multinational companies and financial institutions, which would be passed along in prices or absorbed in lower returns [S2].

Its rebuttable presumptions would treat money moving through banks that don't meet FATCA reporting rules as taxable income unless the taxpayer proves otherwise with 'clear and convincing evidence,' a heavy burden that critics would call unfair to ordinary account holders caught in the net [S3].
Rules targeting countries and banks that 'significantly impede' U.S. tax enforcement give the Treasury broad discretion that trading partners could see as overreach and retaliatory [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and well-documented problem: profits and assets shifted offshore so they are never taxed. The costs fall almost entirely on the companies and individuals using those arrangements, though compliance costs would be real and some enforcement tools are blunt. Nothing in the record indicates an up-or-down debate on these tradeoffs — the bill never got one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act on April 5, 2017, with one Democratic cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and offshore financial providers kept the existing rules, and offshore profit-shifting and asset-hiding arrangements continued untouched. Ordinary taxpayers continued to cover the revenue those arrangements avoid.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (chair Sen. Orrin Hatch)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 5, 2017 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the Republican-run Finance Committee never acted on the bill; no votes were ever held, so the partisan split appears in sponsorship and inaction rather than in the record.

industries.note: The bill limits deductions tied to deferred foreign income, taxes income shifted through intangible transfers, treats U.S.-managed foreign corporations as domestic, and tightens inversion rules — all aimed at profits parked in low-tax countries. These arrangements shift tax burdens onto domestic taxpayers and workers.

industries.industry: Offshore financial and trust service providers
industries.note: Banks in non-cooperating jurisdictions would face restrictions on U.S. correspondent accounts and payment cards, and company formation agents would face anti-money-laundering requirements. Their business depends on secrecy that U.S. enforcement cannot penetrate.

Investment advisers would have to run anti-money-laundering programs, file suspicious activity reports, and identify customers, which may help catch evasion routed through funds. Compliance costs would fall on the industry.
New country-by-country reporting would make profits and taxes paid visible in every jurisdiction, increasing transparency for investors and the public, at the cost of additional reporting work.
